solver.kind: blind AI solver B (separate agent, answer-free packet, adversarial rubric)

E049-01.notes: Colon correctly introduces the explanation of the flaw. B is a comma splice (two independent clauses). C is a fused sentence. D 'a serious flaw, which it tended to pop open' leaves 'which' with no role in its clause, so it is ungrammatical. Fact check on the whole passage: Judson's 1893 clasp-locker patent, Sundback (Swedish-born) at the company holding Judson's patents (Universal Fastener) c. 1913, about two decades later, more teeth per inch (from about 4 to 10-11), 'hookless fastener', and Goodrich's 1923 'Zipper' boots with the president (Bertram Work) linked to the sound are all consistent with the standard account. Small simplifications: Sundback's own patent title was 'Separable Fastener', and 'Hookless' was largely the company and product name. Sales also rose somewhat with WWI-era uses before 1923. Neither is a defect at ACT level.

E049-02.notes: Sentence 4 needs a main verb. A (which used), B (using) and C (that used) all leave 'Sundback's design' without a predicate, so each is a fragment. D supplies 'used' as the main verb, and the 'each shaped...' absolute phrase then attaches correctly.

E049-03.notes: Dangling modifier: the fastener did not increase the teeth. C names Sundback as the agent. B is still dangling, with only the tense changed. D is still dangling and also awkwardly inverted.

E049-04.notes: 'did little to excite' is concise and fits 'Sales stayed modest'. B is redundant (thrill and excite). C 'did a little' reverses the meaning to 'somewhat'. D is unidiomatic.

E049-05.notes: There are two independent clauses with a causal link (he enjoyed the sound, so he named them). A has no comma before 'and', and 'and' weakens the cause-effect relationship, so it is the defended original but is substandard. C 'although' gives an illogical contrast. D is a semicolon followed by a participial fragment.

E049-06.notes: The subject 'Few' is plural, so it takes 'know'. A, B and D are singular, and D also uses the stative 'knowing' unidiomatically. The intervening 'of the people who use them every day' is the intended trap.

flags.note: A is a strong rival. Paragraph 3 fully explains how 'zipper' came about, and the essay also traces earlier names ('clasp locker', 'hookless fastener'), so a student could argue the naming thread runs throughout. D is better because two of the four paragraphs are about mechanism and development, and naming is one paragraph. Still, the A-vs-D distinction depends on the 'primary purpose' convention. It would be worth making the development material even more dominant, or tightening A so it is clearly too narrow.

E049-07.notes: C is factually false, because sentence 9 gives the origin. B gives the wrong reason for 'yes' (the mechanism has nothing to do with the name). D fits the ACT primary-purpose pattern: the name is covered in one paragraph, and the essay as a whole is a history of the device's development.

E049-08.notes: The added sentence about farmers is an off-topic digression between the Goodrich adoption and the naming anecdote. A is wrong because the sentence says nothing about this line of boots selling well. B is wrong because it does not identify first users. D is wrong because there is no contradiction. C's reasoning ('buyers unrelated to the history of the fastener') is slightly broad but correct in context.
